systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.

Rubrique : Climat
Date du flux : 05/11/2026
Auteur : Yuchen Wei; Fang Guo; Yawen Wang; Zihao Guo; Guozhang Lin; Conglu Li; Shi Zhao; Chao Ren; Kin Fai Ho; Eng Kiong Yeoh; Ka Chun Chong
Titre d'origine : Impact of temperature variability on mortality during extreme heat and cold conditions over 20 years: A time-space-stratified case-crossover study

ARTICLE :
Figures
Abstract
Background
Climate change-induced temperature variability poses growing health risks. The effects of this variability on mortality are well established; however, its specific impact during extreme heat and cold conditions remains understudied. This represents a knowledge gap, as the human body’s physiological capacity to adapt to sudden temperature shifts is compromised when ambient temperatures are extreme. To address this, our study examined the relationship between mortality and temperature variability in Hong Kong for a 21-year period.
Methods
A time-space-stratified case-crossover design was used in this study. Daily weather data from ERA5-Land and PM2.5 levels from ChinaHighPM2.5 were combined with mortality records in Hong Kong from 2000 to 2020. Diurnal temperature range (DTR) and temperature changes between consecutive days (TCN) were used as the temperature variability metrics. Extreme hot and cold conditions were defined by annual temperature percentiles: > 75%, > 90%, > 95%, > 97.5% for hot seasons, and <25%, < 10%, < 5%, < 2.5% for cold seasons. A conditional logistic regression was used to examine the association between temperature variability metrics and mortality, adjusting for other environmental factors. Subgroup analyses by age and cause-specific mortality were performed.
Results
DTR and TCN were strongly associated with mortality during heat extremes. For temperatures >97.5th percentile, DTR (odds ratio [OR] = 1.99, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.90-2.08) and TCN (OR = 2.24, 95% CI: 2.09-2.40) showed increased risks for all-cause mortality. During cold extremes (<2.5th percentile), DTR showed an inverse association (OR = 0.93, 95% CI: 0.90-0.95), while TCN was associated with increased odds of all-cause mortality (OR = 1.06, 95% CI: 1.04-1.08).
Conclusion
Temperature variability was associated with an increased risk of mortality during extreme heat conditions, with mortality risk rising alongside higher extreme temperature levels, while during extreme cold, the associations were generally smaller. At temperatures above the 97.5th percentile, each 1°C increase in DTR and TCN was associated with approximately 99% and 124% higher odds of all-cause mortality, respectively. These findings highlight the need for targeted public health strategies to protect vulnerable populations from climate-induced temperature fluctuations.

Background
Climate change poses an escalating threat to human health across generations, causing significant disruptions to environmental and social systems [1,2]. Alongside climate change, extreme temperatures emerge as the most pervasive and significant challenge to public health worldwide, leading to substantial excess mortality [3]. Extreme temperatures can lead to organ-specific thermoregulatory failure, primarily through electrolyte imbalances and the exacerbation of pre-existing conditions. This has been linked to various adverse health outcomes, such as cardiovascular, respiratory, and maternal diseases [4–6].
In addition to the intensity of extreme temperatures, the frequency and magnitude of temperature variability—both inter-day and intra-day—have also increased alongside climate change [7]. Epidemiological studies have shown the impact of short-term temperature variation on health outcomes, including intra- and inter-day temperature variation [8–11]. Rapid temperature fluctuations demand continuous physiological adjustments, placing stress on the autonomic nervous system and exacerbating cardiovascular and respiratory strain [12,13]. As temperature varies rapidly over short periods, individuals may not be able to physiologically adapt to sudden temperature changes [14]. According to the global estimates in a modelling study [11], approximately 1.7 million deaths were related to temperature variability each year from 2000 to 2019, with Asia being one of the regions observed to have the highest percentage of excess mortality. In these studies, DTR is typically used as an intra-day temperature variation indicator, whereas TCN is used as an inter-day indicator. The associations of both DTR and TCN with mortality have been well established in numerous studies [8–11,15].
Despite extensive independent research on extreme temperatures and temperature variability separately, their combined epidemiological impact remains insufficiently understood. Specifically, it remains unclear whether the mortality associations with inter-day and intra-day temperature variability become stronger as ambient temperatures become more extreme. Considering that a sudden heat or cold variation may be less efficiently adapted to by human physiology when temperatures become extreme, we hypothesized that greater temperature variability would have a stronger adverse association with mortality under more extreme conditions. Furthermore, densely populated subtropical cities like Hong Kong are particularly vulnerable to these combined temperature conditions, as Hong Kong is facing the compounding challenges of a rapidly aging population and a significant urban heat island effect [16]. In this study, we examined the association of temperature variability (DTR and TCN) during extreme heat and cold conditions with all-cause mortality, as well as cause-specific mortality in Hong Kong over a 21-year period. By jointly evaluating two complementary temperature-variability metrics across multiple extreme-temperature thresholds, our study extends previous research that generally considered temperature variability and extreme temperature separately and provides evidence relevant to heat-health risk assessment.
Methods
Ethics statement
This is a retrospective study using anonymous individual-level data from the Death Registry of Hong Kong, accessed on August 6, 2024. Ethics approval was obtained from the Joint CUHK-NTEC Clinical Research Ethics Committee (No. 2024.344). Because this is a retrospective study, informed consent was waived by the ethics committee.
Data sources
Daily mortality data were collected from the Death Registry of Hong Kong for the 2000–2020 period. The dataset included the date of death, residential address code in Tertiary Planning Unit (TPU), cause of death (coded by ICD-9 or ICD-10), age, and sex. All-cause mortality was used as the main outcome, while cause-specific mortality was further assessed in the subgroup analysis. Mortality caused by cardiovascular diseases was classified using ICD-9 code 390–459 or ICD-10 code I00-I99. Mortality caused by respiratory disease was classified using ICD-9 code 460–519 or ICD-10 code J00-J99. Mortality caused by injury was classified using ICD-9 code 800–999, E and V codes or ICD-10 code V01-Y98 [17–19].
We used the ERA5-Land dataset with 0.1° x 0.1° (approximately 9 km) horizontal resolution to extract grid-level hourly weather factors [20], including air temperature, dew point temperature, and wind speed. The daily PM2.5 was retrieved from the ChinaHighPM2.5 dataset with approximately 1 km resolution during the study period [21]. The meteorological variables and air pollutant levels were averaged and mapped to each TPU [22] on a daily basis. Kriging interpolation using the 10 closest grids was applied to estimate any missing data.
Temperature variability
The temperature variability was assessed using the diurnal temperature range (DTR) and temperature change between neighboring days (TCN). Statistical analysis
Data were analysed using conditional logistic regression. Control days were chosen as 7 days before, 7 days after, and 14 days after the case day. These intervals preserved day of the week while keeping referent days close to the case day, thereby limiting confounding by rapidly changing seasonal conditions in a subtropical climate. Case and control days were matched within the same TPU; therefore, relatively stable TPU-level spatial characteristics were controlled by design. Several environmental covariates were adjusted, including ambient temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and PM2.5 levels. A simplified conceptual directed acyclic graph illustrating the assumed relationships among temperature variability, meteorological covariates, PM2.5, and mortality is provided in S1 Fig. To better account for the potential exposure-lag effects of these covariates, a Distributed Lag Non-Linear Model (DLNM) [23] was applied using a natural cubic spline function with a lag period of up to 7 days. DTR and TCN were entered as same-day linear terms because the estimand was the acute association between variability and mortality on the day already classified as extreme; DTR summarizes within-day variability, and TCN incorporates temperatures on the current and preceding days. Odds ratios (ORs) per unit increase in DTR and TCN with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. The association between temperature variability and mortality was analysed under different levels of extreme temperature conditions for the hot and cold seasons separately. Days exceeding the 75th, 90th, 95th, and 97.5th annual temperature percentiles during the hot season were included in the analysis. For the cold season, days below the 25th, 10th, 5th, and 2.5th annual temperature percentiles were extracted to account for extremely low temperature conditions. The temperature percentiles were calculated annually, based on the distribution of daily mean temperatures for each individual year within the study period. The percentile cutoffs were selected to span moderate to very extreme temperature conditions while retaining sufficient observations at each level. These nested definitions were used to describe the associations across progressively more extreme temperature conditions. If a mortality case occurred on an extreme temperature day, the case day and its corresponding control days were selected for comparison. A subgroup analysis was conducted by age groups: 0–49, 50–64, 65–79 and 80 years and above. For sensitivity analysis, the year 2020 was excluded from the analysis to account for potential mortality influences from the Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. Furthermore, we conducted a sensitivity analysis in which control days were selected using the “same day of the week within the same month” approach to ensure the robustness of results.
Results
Between 2000 and 2020, 852,529 deaths were recorded in Hong Kong. Among the total deaths, 23.92% were attributed to cardiovascular diseases, 20.40% to respiratory diseases, and 3.84% to injuries or external causes. Mean daily ambient temperatures of 27.69°C (Standard Deviation [SD]: 2.11) and 19.53°C (SD: 3.76) were recorded during hot and cold seasons, respectively. The mean DTR was 4.12°C (SD: 1.31) in hot seasons and 5.40°C (SD: 2.11) in cold seasons (Table 1). For TCN, median values of 0.10°C were observed during hot seasons, with ranges from 5.31°C decrease to 3.30°C increase. During cold seasons, median TCN values of 0.29°C were recorded, ranging from 6.30°C decrease to 11.43°C increase. The detailed calendar heatmaps of annual temperature extremes are shown in S2-S5 Fig.
The association between temperature variability and all-cause mortality was evaluated across different ambient temperature percentiles for hot and cold seasons (Fig 1 and S1 Table). In the hot season, temperature variability was positively associated with all-cause mortality at higher ambient temperature percentiles. For DTR, the ORs increased progressively when temperature exceeded the 75th (1.17, 95% CI: 1.16-1.18), 90th (1.33, 95% CI: 1.31-1.35), 95th (1.42, 95% CI: 1.39-1.45), and 97.5th (1.99, 95% CI: 1.90-2.08) percentiles. TCN also showed a positive association with all-cause mortality at higher percentiles. At temperatures above the 97.5th percentile, the OR was 2.24 (95% CI: 2.09-2.40). In the cold season, DTR was observed to be negatively associated with mortality at lower ambient temperature percentiles, including the 25th (0.92, 95% CI: 0.92-0.92), 10th (0.85, 95% CI: 0.85-0.86), 5th (0.79, 95% CI: 0.78-0.80), and 2.5th (0.93, 95% CI: 0.90-0.95) percentiles. TCN showed a marginally significant positive association with mortality across different cold temperature conditions.
The association between temperature variability and all-cause mortality showed a broadly similar pattern across age groups (Fig 2 and S2 Table). During the hot season, temperature variability associated mortality risk increased with temperature. For example, among individuals aged 80 and above, ORs for TCN were 1.26 (95% CI: 1.23-1.30) when the temperature was higher than the 90th percentile, 1.46 (95% CI: 1.39-1.53) when higher than the 95th percentile, and 2.19 (95% CI: 2.00-2.40) when higher than the 97.5th percentile. Across the other age groups, ORs ranged from 1.13 (95% CI: 1.09-1.16) to 2.58 (95% CI: 1.89-3.53) under extreme temperature conditions. DTR also showed a positive association with mortality, though with smaller effect sizes compared to TCN. In the cold season, DTR showed a negative association with mortality at low ambient temperature conditions across age groups. For the 80 + group, ORs for DTR were 0.85 (95% CI: 0.84-0.86) when temperature was lower than the 10th percentile, 0.84 (95% CI: 0.82-0.85) when lower than the 5th percentile, and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.84-0.92) when lower than the 2.5th percentile. TCN showed limited or marginal significance across all age groups during cold seasons.
Mortality risk associated with DTR and TCN progressively increased under higher temperature conditions. When temperatures exceeded the 95th percentile, ORs for DTR reached 1.47 (95% CI: 1.41-1.54), 1.54 (95% CI: 1.46-1.61), and 1.42 (95% CI: 1.27-1.59), and the corresponding ORs for TCN were 1.45 (95% CI: 1.35-1.55), 1.53 (95% CI: 1.42-1.65), and 1.66 (95% CI: 1.39-1.98) for cardiovascular disease (CVD), respiratory, and injury-related deaths, respectively (Fig 3 and S3 Table). In the cold season, DTR showed an inverse association with mortality. When temperatures were below the 2.5th percentile, TCN was associated with CVD-related mortality (OR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.01-1.20) and respiratory-related mortality (OR = 1.12, 95% CI: 1.06-1.17), indicating the adverse effects of continuously dropping temperatures. However, DTR exhibited no clear pattern of association for these causes.
To account for potential mortality influences from the COVID-19 pandemic, the year 2020 was excluded from the analysis. The results remained robust and unchanged, confirming the stability of the findings despite the removal of data from this period. In addition, when employing the “same day of the week within the same month” approach for control day selection, the estimated effects of temperature variability on mortality remained highly consistent with our main results (S6 Fig).
Discussion
Climate change is exacerbating both the frequency and intensity of extreme temperature events, thereby elevating risks to human health. While the literature has extensively studied the adverse impacts of temperature variability, few studies have investigated the potential intensified effect on human health during extreme cold or heat conditions. Our study employed more than 20 years of mortality data in Hong Kong, a subtropical setting experiencing changing patterns of extreme weather each year. We primarily demonstrated that temperature variability was associated with an increased risk of mortality during extreme heat conditions, with mortality risk rising alongside higher extreme temperature levels. In contrast, the associations between temperature variability and mortality during extreme cold conditions were less pronounced than those observed under extreme heat scenarios. The increasing risk associated with temperature variability under hotter extreme conditions showed broadly similar descriptive patterns across different age groups and major disease subgroups including CVD, respiratory diseases, and injuries. Given the implications of climate change, our findings highlight that the health burden associated with temperature variability—often overlooked compared to other environmental factors—should be addressed in future health policies aimed at combating extreme weather events. Specifically, public health authorities should consider integrating temperature variability metrics (such as DTR and TCN) into existing heat-health warning systems to trigger early alerts.
Our study showed that both inter-day and intra-day temperature variability were linked to a higher risk of mortality during extreme heat conditions, with the risk increasing as extreme temperature levels rose. We speculated that extremely high temperature conditions likely disrupt the body’s ability to regulate internal temperature, potentially leading to dehydration, while a sudden rapid change in temperature may further induce stress on the thermoregulatory system [24]. In addition, extreme heat can lead to heat stress, causing physical and cognitive abnormalities (e.g., fatigue and dizziness), and fluctuating temperatures may additionally exacerbate the symptoms for those whose thermoregulation abilities have already been diminished. In fact, Wu et al. suggested that temperature variability likely modifies the extreme heat-mortality association, with an increased risk of heat-related mortality observed in conjunction with increases in temperature variability [25]. Furthermore, Lee et al. demonstrated that the mortality risk associated with temperature variability was modified by different temperature levels, ranging from extremely cold to extremely hot, for all causes and cardiovascular deaths [26]. Their results are consistent with our findings on CVD deaths. However, we observed a more pronounced risk gradient at the extreme upper temperature percentiles. The observation in our study is possibly due to Hong Kong’s high-density urban morphology [16], which may further compromise physiological heat dissipation when rapid temperature fluctuations occur.
In our study, DTR was associated with lower odds of mortality during extreme cold conditions, and these associations were less pronounced than those observed in extreme heat scenarios. As Hong Kong is a subtropical location with average winter temperatures ranging from 15 to 19oC, one possible explanation is that extreme cold days are generally ‘warmer’ compared to those in temperate regions (e.g., the cooler region in Japan [26]), which may partly explain the smaller associations observed for temperature variability. In this subtropical context, a larger DTR during an extreme cold event may indicate that while nighttime temperatures are low, daytime temperatures rise back to a comfortable level. This daytime warming may reduce the overall duration of physiological cold stress. Furthermore, behavioral adaptations, such as adding clothing or bedding, may help individuals cope with nighttime cold and could contribute to the observed inverse association. However, this explanation could not be directly assessed because data on indoor temperature, heating use, clothing, and time-activity patterns were unavailable, and other mechanisms may also contribute. The J-shaped relationships between temperature and mortality over different quartiles of temperature variability from Wu et al. [25] provide some context that the temperature-variability effect remains consistent during extremely cold days. Nevertheless, the factors contributing to the more pronounced mortality impacts related to temperature variability during extreme hot conditions, compared to extreme cold, are varied. One general explanation is that individuals are more capable of coping with cold (e.g., clothing) than with extreme heat. Additionally, higher temperatures are also associated with worsening air quality, particularly the increased ozone levels, which remain a pollution concern in Hong Kong and are associated with respiratory health outcomes [27]. The physiological heterogeneity in responses to temperature variability under extreme heat and cold conditions warrants further exploration.
A major strength of this study is the use of long-term mortality data (i.e., 21 years), which are highly representative since the Hong Kong death registry database includes full coverage of local deaths under ordinance and has ensured data quality through regular auditing. Nevertheless, there are several limitations in this study. First, the study does not account for time-varying behaviors during extreme temperatures, such as changes in indoor heating use, time spent outdoors, or clothing choices, which could significantly influence individual exposure levels. Second, while several temperature variability metrics have been studied in the literature, we were unable to investigate all of them in our study. However, our primary finding remains generally robust when using several other temperature variability metrics. PM2.5 was included as an a priori time-varying environmental covariate, but other pollutants such as ozone, nitrogen dioxide, and sulfur dioxide were unavailable at the required spatial and temporal coverage; residual confounding by air pollution is therefore possible. Third, since the cause-of-death classification in our study was based on ICD-9 or ICD-10 codes, potential misclassification bias should be acknowledged. Fourth, although case days and control days were compared within the same TPU, thereby controlling for relatively stable TPU-level characteristics, the study design did not directly assess whether the associations differed between TPUs. Future studies using TPU-specific estimates or interaction terms, together with detailed urban-form indicators, are warranted to examine potential geographic variation. In addition, residential TPU-level exposure estimates do not capture individual mobility, indoor temperature, heating or air-conditioning use, clothing, or time spent outdoors. ERA5-Land has a 0.1° grid and therefore cannot resolve all microclimatic variation arising from urban form, topography, and coastal influences. This exposure error would be expected to reduce spatial and temporal contrast, but the magnitude and direction of bias in the association estimates cannot be quantified without an independent local validation dataset. Fifth, because Hong Kong is a densely populated subtropical city, our findings may not generalize to regions with different climates, urban environments or demographics. Further multi-city studies are needed to confirm these associations in other settings.
Conclusion
In conclusion, our study demonstrated that temperature variability was associated with an increased risk of mortality during extreme heat conditions, with mortality risk rising alongside higher extreme temperature levels. At temperatures above the 97.5th percentile, each 1°C increase in DTR and TCN was associated with approximately 99% and 124% higher odds of all-cause mortality, respectively. During extreme cold, the associations were generally smaller and differed between DTR and TCN. From a public health perspective, these findings emphasize the need to integrate temperature variability into existing climate-health policies. Current heat-health warning systems should be refined to account for rapid temperature fluctuations. Furthermore, raising public awareness about sudden temperature shifts is vital to protect vulnerable populations, including older adults and individuals with cardiovascular or respiratory conditions, from escalating climate extremes.
